newsitem.title: UK: Father of the Brady market foresees its demise.
newsitem.headline: Father of the Brady market foresees its demise.

text.p: Nicholas Brady, the father of the Brady bond plan that restored credibility to Latin America after the 1980s debt crisis, on Monday forecast the demise of the market that bears his name.

"I hope all Bradys go through the process, where the country stands on its own two feet," he said. "It's a sign of progress." Speaking to London financiers at a conference on Latin America run by the Templeton Investment Trust, he said talk that Mexico was buying back its Brady bonds with the proceeds from its global bond issues was positive.
"It is a good thing for the country," he said.

Mexico has set a precedent in attempting to retire its collateralised Brady bonds -- restructured commercial debt issued to replace defaulted commercial loans of the 1980s -- after launching 30 and 20-year global bonds earlier this year.

Earlier on Monday, the Philippines completed the exchange of its 2017 and 2018 Brady bonds for new 20-year fixed rate bonds, which lack the Bradys' stigma of default. This month, Brazil's Congress passed a bill allowing the country to swap restructured Brady debt for global bonds and market players speculate whether Argentina and Venezuela might follow suit.
Brady said the financial future of the region was already beginning to rest in the hands of equity investors.

"The region badly needs funds and the day is way behind us when commercial banks will provide the funds, while the World Bank and the IMF simply don't have enough money to put in," he said. "It's an equity problem...it's an equity risk that has to he undertaken by equity holders."

He said capital flows were still crucial to fuel growth for investment, productivity and a population with a higher standard of living and political reforms opening up the regions' economies were vital.
"Reform is a key part of it and I wonder whether countries are getting a bit forgetful about it," he said. "The leaders of these countries will have to face the music."
But he said he was confident about their commitment to making the reform movement work.

"The leaders have been educated in the best schools of Britain, France and the United States, they are familiar with economic theories and they are going to continue to make the reform movement work," he said.

As investors brace for Tuesday's crucial meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve policymakers, which may result in a U.S. interest rate rise of 25 basis points, he said any upwards move would not be good for Latin America where the effect will be magnified.

"It's not a good thing for the region if the Fed raises rates," he said. "With high interest rates, people don't invest as much for instance in industry and that is echoed in spades in Latin America, where rates will be that much higher."
